summary: This mishnah teaches how many judges are needed for different kinds of court cases about money and fines. Rabbi Meir and the Sages argue about one case that might end in a death penalty.

chunks.en: Cases about money are judged by three judges.
chunks.st: Cases concerning monetary law are adjudicated by three judges.

words.note: Court cases.
Three judges.

chunks.en: Cases of stealing and of hurting someone are judged by three.
chunks.st: Cases concerning robbery and personal injury are adjudicated by three judges.

chunks.en: Cases of full damage and half damage,
chunks.st: Cases concerning damage that one is responsible for because he or his property caused the damage are adjudicated by three judges as well. Likewise, cases concerning payment for half the damage,
chunks.stMore: which is paid in the event that an ox whose owner has not been warned that it gored more than two times gores another animal (see Exodus 21:35);

words.note: Paying for harm that a person or his animal did.
An ox that was not known to gore pays only half.

chunks.he: תַּשְׁלוּמֵי כֶפֶל וְתַשְׁלוּמֵי אַרְבָּעָה וַחֲמִשָּׁה, בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה.
chunks.en: paying double, and paying four or five times, are judged by three.
chunks.st: cases concerning payment of double the principal by a thief who was caught stealing (see Exodus 22:3); and cases concerning payment of four or five times the principal by a thief who slaughtered or sold a stolen ox or a lamb (see Exodus 21:37) are all adjudicated by three judges.

words.note: A thief who is caught pays back double.
A thief who sold or slaughtered a stolen ox or sheep.

chunks.en: Cases of fines for wronging a girl, and of a man who says a false bad thing about his wife, are judged by three,
chunks.st: Cases concerning one who rapes or one who seduces a virgin girl, and must therefore pay the girl’s father fifty silver shekels (see Deuteronomy 22:29, Exodus 22:15); and cases concerning a defamer who falsely asserts that his wife was not a virgin when she married him, and brings false witnesses who testify that she committed adultery while betrothed to him and who must therefore pay the girl’s father one hundred silver shekels as well as receive lashes (see Deuteronomy 22:13–19): All of these are adjudicated by three judges;

words.note: He did a terrible wrong to a girl and must pay a fine.
He also did a wrong to a girl and must pay a fine.
A husband who falsely says his new wife did a sin.

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.en: the case of the one who says a false bad thing about his wife is judged by twenty-three,
chunks.st: Cases concerning a defamer are adjudicated by a court of twenty-three
chunks.stMore: judges, which is the type of court authorized to judge cases of capital law,

chunks.en: because it may turn into a case of life and death.
chunks.explain: If his wife were found guilty, she could get a death penalty.
chunks.st: because this case includes the possibility of becoming a case of capital law.
chunks.stMore: The husband brings witnesses that his wife committed adultery. If she is found guilty, she is liable to receive the death penalty. This punishment applies to the witnesses if they are exposed as conspiring witnesses.

summary: How many judges are needed to give lashes, and to add an extra day to a month or an extra month to a year? Rabbi Meir says three, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains how the judges for a leap year are added.
stIntro: Cases concerning the violation of prohibitions that render one liable to receive

chunks.st: lashes are adjudicated by three judges.

words.note: A punishment of being hit with a strap.

chunks.st: Cases concerning lashes are adjudicated by twenty-three judges.

chunks.en: Making a month longer is done by three.
chunks.st: The intercalation of the month is performed by a panel of three judges.

words.note: Adding a thirtieth day to the month.

chunks.en: Making a year longer is done by three,
chunks.st: The intercalation of the year, meaning the decision to add an extra month to the year when necessary, is also decided by a panel of three judges;

words.note: Adding an extra month, to make a leap year.

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says,
chunks.st: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

chunks.en: they start with three,

chunks.en: And if they finished with three, it is a leap year.
chunks.st: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concedes that if they concluded the matter with only three judges, the intercalation is valid and it is a leap year.

summary: This mishnah lists more things a court of three or more judges must do, like giving semichah, the egla arufah, chalitzah, and setting the value of things given to the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: Giving semichah to elders, and breaking the calf's neck,
chunks.st: Both the laying of hands by the Sages and the breaking of the heifer’s neck
chunks.stMore: in a case where a person was found murdered and it is not known who killed him (see Deuteronomy 21:1–9)

words.note: Giving semichah, making someone a judge.
The egla arufah, done when a murdered person is found and no one knows who killed him.

chunks.en: are done with three. That is what Rabbi Shimon says.
chunks.st: are performed in front of a panel of three judges; this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Yehudah says, with five.
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: These rituals are performed in front of five judges.

chunks.en: Chalitzah and mi'un are done with three.
chunks.st: Both ḥalitza, the ritual through which the yavam, a surviving brother of a married man who died without sons, frees the yevama, the widow, of her levirate bond in a case where the yavam does not wish to marry the yevama (see Deuteronomy 25:5–10), and the refusal of a girl before reaching majority to remain married to the man to whom her mother or brother married her off, are performed before a court of three
chunks.stMore: judges. The halakha concerning fruit of a fourth-year sapling and second-tithe produce is that they are to be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there. If this is impractical, the produce can be redeemed and the redemption money brought to Jerusalem, where it is used to purchase food and drink.

words.note: Freeing a widow from marrying her husband's brother.
A young girl saying she does not want to stay married.

chunks.en: Fruit of a fourth-year tree and maaser sheni

Second tithe, also eaten in Yerushalayim.

chunks.en: whose price is not known are valued by three.
chunks.st: where their value is not known is performed by three judges.

chunks.en: Things given to hekdesh are valued by three.
chunks.st: The valuation of consecrated property for purposes of redemption is performed by three judges,

words.note: Things given to the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: Erech payments of movable things are valued by three.
chunks.st: and the valuations that are movable property (see Leviticus 27:1–8) are performed by three judges.

words.note: Money a person promised to the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: one of them must be a Kohen.
chunks.st: One of the three judges must be a priest.

chunks.en: And land is valued by nine and a Kohen.
chunks.st: And the valuation of consecrated land is performed by nine judges and, in addition, one priest.

chunks.en: And a person is valued the same way as land.
chunks.st: And the valuation of a person for the purpose of a vow is performed in a similar manner to that of land.

summary: The great Sanhedrin had seventy-one judges and a small Sanhedrin had twenty-three. The mishnah shows from pesukim where each number comes from, and how big a city must be to have a Sanhedrin.
stIntro: With regard to the number of judges in the different courts the mishna presents a halakhic midrash:

chunks.he: סַנְהֶדְרִי גְדוֹלָה הָיְתָה שֶׁל שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד,
chunks.en: The great Sanhedrin had seventy-one judges,
chunks.st: The Great Sanhedrin was composed of seventy-one judges,

chunks.en: and the small one had twenty-three.
chunks.st: and a lesser Sanhedrin was composed of twenty-three.

chunks.he: וּמִנַּיִן לַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁהִיא שֶׁל שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד,
chunks.en: And how do we know that the great one has seventy-one?
chunks.st: From where is it derived that the Great Sanhedrin was composed of seventy-one judges?

chunks.en: As it says, "Gather for Me
chunks.st: As it is stated: “Gather Me

chunks.en: seventy men from the elders of Yisrael,"
chunks.st: seventy men of the Elders of Israel,
chunks.stMore: whom you know to be the Elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them into the Tent of Meeting, and they shall stand there with you” (Numbers 11:16),

chunks.en: and Moshe is over them.
chunks.st: and together with Moses at the head of this body,

chunks.en: That makes seventy-one.
chunks.st: there are a total of seventy-one.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says, seventy.
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: Moses was indeed at the head of the body, but he is not counted as part of the group. Consequently, a future Great Sanhedrin modeled after these Elders is to be composed of seventy judges.

chunks.he: וּמִנַּיִן לַקְּטַנָּה שֶׁהִיא שֶׁל עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה,
chunks.en: And how do we know that the small one has twenty-three?
chunks.st: And from where is it derived that a lesser Sanhedrin is composed of twenty-three judges?

chunks.en: As it says,
chunks.st: As it is stated:

chunks.en: "And the congregation shall judge..."
chunks.st: “And the congregation shall judge between the assailant and the avenger…

chunks.en: "and the congregation shall save."
chunks.st: and the congregation shall save
chunks.stMore: the manslayer from the hands of the avenger” (Numbers 35:24–25).

chunks.en: A group that judges, and a group that saves.
chunks.explain: One group tries to find him guilty, and one tries to save him.
chunks.st: Therefore, there must be a congregation, which consists of at least ten judges, that judges the accused and attempts to convict him, and there must be a congregation, also consisting of at least ten judges, which attempts to save the accused by finding him innocent.

chunks.en: That makes twenty.
chunks.st: Together, there are twenty judges here.
chunks.stMore: Before proceeding to derive the requirement for the final three judges, the mishna clarifies:

chunks.en: And how do we know that a "congregation" is ten?
chunks.st: And from where is it derived that a congregation consists of at least ten men?

chunks.en: As it says
chunks.st: As it is stated concerning the spies:

chunks.en: "How long for this bad congregation,"
chunks.explain: Hashem said this about the spies.
chunks.st: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation
chunks.stMore: that keep complaining about me?” (Numbers 14:27) There were twelve spies;

chunks.en: without Yehoshua and Kalev.
chunks.explain: There were twelve spies; without these two, there were ten.
chunks.st: excluding Joshua and Caleb,
chunks.stMore: who did not complain, there would be ten men who are called: A congregation. Accordingly, the verses describing a congregation that attempts to convict the accused and a congregation that attempts to acquit him together add up to twenty judges.

chunks.en: And how do we know to add three more?
chunks.st: And from where is it derived to bring three more judges to the court?

chunks.en: From what it says,
chunks.st: From the implication of that which is stated:

chunks.en: "Do not follow the many to do bad,"
chunks.st: “You shall not follow a multitude to convict” (Exodus 23:2),

chunks.en: I hear that I may go with them to do good.
chunks.st: I would derive that I may not convict a person on the basis of a majority but I should follow the majority to exonerate.

chunks.en: If so, why does it say,
chunks.st: If so, why is it stated in the same verse:

chunks.en: "Lean after the many"?
chunks.st: “To incline after a multitude,”
chunks.stMore: from which it can be understood that the majority is followed in all cases? In order to resolve the apparent contradiction it must be explained:

chunks.en: Leaning to good is not like leaning to bad.
chunks.st: Your inclination after the majority to exonerate is not like your inclination after the majority to convict.

chunks.en: To lean to good, one more judge is enough.
chunks.st: Your inclination after the majority to exonerate can result in a verdict by a majority of one judge.

chunks.en: To lean to bad, you need two more.
chunks.st: But your inclination after the majority to convict a transgressor must be by a more decisive majority of at least two.
chunks.stMore: Therefore, the court must have at least twenty-two judges.

chunks.en: And a court may not be an even number,
chunks.st: And since there is a principle that a court may not be composed of an even
chunks.stMore: number of judges, as such a court may be unable to reach a decision, therefore

words.note: A number that can be split into two equal halves.

chunks.en: so we add one more judge.
chunks.st: they add another one to them, and

chunks.en: That makes twenty-three.
chunks.st: there are twenty-three judges here.

chunks.he: וְכַמָּה יְהֵא בְעִיר וּתְהֵא רְאוּיָה לְסַנְהֶדְרִין,
chunks.en: How many people must be in a city for it to have a Sanhedrin?
chunks.st: And how many men must be in the city for it to be eligible for a lesser Sanhedrin?

chunks.en: A hundred and twenty.
chunks.st: One hundred and twenty.

chunks.en: Rabbi Nechemyah says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Neḥemya says:

chunks.en: two hundred and thirty,
chunks.st: Two hundred and thirty,

chunks.en: to match the leaders of tens.
chunks.explain: Each judge should have at least ten people to lead.
chunks.st: corresponding to the ministers of tens,
chunks.stMore: as outlined by Moses and Yitro in the wilderness (Exodus, chapter 18). That is to say, each member of the Sanhedrin can be viewed as a judge with responsibility for ten residents. If there are not enough men in the city to enable this calculation, it would not be honorable to appoint a Sanhedrin, as their members will each preside over less than the minimum of ten residents.
